    What is R?

    R is a language and environment for statistical computing and graphics.

    It is free.

    It is open-source. meaning that the original source code* is made freely available and may be redistributed and modified.

    R uses syntax, which means that, to “speak” the language, you’ll need to program/code.

    R provides a wide variety of statistical and graphical techniques and is highly extensible. One of R’s strengths is the ease with which well-designed publication-quality plots can be produced and adapted, including mathematical symbols and formulae where needed. R is available as Free Software under the terms of the Free Software Foundation’s GNU General Public License. It compiles and runs on a wide variety of platforms and similar systems including Linux, Windows, and MacOS.

    R is an integrated suite of software facilities for data manipulation, calculation, and graphical display. It includes:

    • an effective data handling and storage facility,
    • a suite of operators for calculations on arrays, in particular matrices,
    • graphical facilities for data analysis and display either on-screen or on hardcopy,
    • and many more

    The R Environment

    The term “environment” is intended to characterize it as a fully planned and coherent system, rather than an incremental mass of very specific and inflexible tools, as is frequently the case with other data analysis software.

    Many users think of R as a statistics system. We prefer to think of it as an environment within which statistical techniques are implemented. R can be extended (easily) via packages. There are about eight packages supplied with the R distribution and many more are available through the CRAN family of Internet sites covering a very wide range of modern statistics.

    What is R Studio?

    RStudio is an Integrated Development Environment (IDE) for R, a programming language for statistical computing and graphics. It is available in two formats: RStudio Desktop is a regular desktop application while RStudio Server runs on a remote server and allows accessing RStudio using a web browser.

    *Source-code: human-readable programming language designed to facilitate actions to be performed by the computer mostly. What’s happening behind the curtains, what makes the program work.

    Mathematical Operators

    • + is for addition
    • - is for subtraction
    • * is for multiplication
    • / is for division
    • ^ or ** is for exponentiation
    x <- 7
y <- 12

x+y

    ## [1] 19

    x-y

    ## [1] -5

    x*y

    ## [1] 84

    y/x

    ## [1] 1.714286

    y**x

    ## [1] 35831808

    y^x

    ## [1] 35831808

    Relational Operators

    • < is for less than
    • > is for greater than
    • == is for equal to
    • <= is for less than or equal to
    • >= is for greater than or equal to
    • != NOT equal to
    x<y

    ## [1] TRUE

    x>y

    ## [1] FALSE

    x<=4

    ## [1] FALSE

    y>=19

    ## [1] FALSE

    y == 12

    ## [1] TRUE

    x != 7

    ## [1] FALSE

    Logical Operators

    • ! is for NOT
    • & is for element-wise AND
    • && is for AND
    • | is for element-wise OR
    • || is for OR
    if (x==7&y==12) print('TRUE')

    ## [1] "TRUE"

    a<-c(5,3,2)
b<-c(4,6,7)

#Don't do this:

if (a == c(5,3,2) | b == c(5,3,2)) print('TRUE')

    ## Error in if (a == c(5, 3, 2) | b == c(5, 3, 2)) print("TRUE"): the condition has length > 1

    #Do this: reduce each comparison to a single TRUE/FALSE first (e.g., with any() or all()),
#then combine them with ||
if (any(a == c(5,3,2)) || any(b == c(5,3,2))) print('TRUE')

    ## [1] "TRUE"

    if (x&y == c(5,3,2)) print('TRUE')

    ## Error in if (x & y == c(5, 3, 2)) print("TRUE"): the condition has length > 1

    if (x&&y == c(5,3,2)) print('TRUE')

    ## Error in x && y == c(5, 3, 2): 'length = 3' in coercion to 'logical(1)'

    Note: older versions of R only gave a warning here and quietly used the first element. Since R 4.2 (for if) and R 4.3 (for && and ||), a condition with more than one element is an error, so make sure every condition you test is a single TRUE or FALSE.

    Order of Operations (BEDMAS)

    4 - 5 + 6 / 2^5*(4+7)

    ## [1] 1.0625

    #If you want to change the order of execution, use round brackets. E.g., 

(4 - 5 + 6) / 2^5*(4+7)

    ## [1] 1.71875

    Left to right associativity

    4 / 7 / 3 / 6

    ## [1] 0.03174603

    #Again, use round brackets to change the order of execution:

4 / (7 / 3) / 6

    ## [1] 0.2857143

    Progress in Module 1

    There are three main types of data objects you may be working with in R: scalars, vectors, and matrices. The simplest of these is a scalar, which is essentially any input that produces a single value as its output.

    There are a few ways to input a scalar object. The first and most simple would be to assign a single value to an object.

    a <- 2

    We can also define a scalar as the result of a numeric problem.

    b <- (90 + 110)

    If we were to run this code and select 'b' we would get a scalar value of '200'.

    Since we have defined 'a' and 'b' as numeric values, we can also create a scalar object by performing operations with these objects.

    c <- b/a
d <- b*a

    This way we can define c as the result of 'b' divided by 'a', and 'd' as the product of 'b' times 'a'. In both cases, a single scalar result will be produced. As well, were we to change the value of 'a' or 'b' – for example, if we changed 'a' to be 5, rather than 2, rerunning 'c' and 'd' would produce updated results.

    Scalars may also be defined as strings or character variables by including quotes around the values.

    e <- '1'

    However, because it is now a string, rather than a numeric value, if we were to attempt to use 'e' in an equation, we would simply receive an error because it is not recognized as a number in this form. Because of this, we can also create strings of letters or words, which may be useful for storing something like labels or names.

    e <- 'potatoes'

    Now 'e' will be a character scalar that reads 'potatoes'.

    From scalars, we can expand to vectors, which can store multiple scalars in a one-dimensional list object. Again, there are multiple ways of doing this. Building off of what we learned about scalars, we may choose to generate vectors by directly defining lists using the c() function. When using c(), you will want to separate each unique value with a comma.

    # c() may use lists of numbers or scalar objects which are pre-defined and may be numeric or strings
count <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
# or 
a <- "potatoes"
b <- "cheese"
c <- "garlic"
d <- "parsley"
e <- "butter"
ingredients <- c(a, b, c, d, e)

    'count' is now defined as a list from 1 to 5 numeric values, while selecting and running 'ingredients' will produce a list of ingredients. The latter method is longer; however, it is easier to edit later if these values will be called upon individually later on.

    Another important note is that vectors can be either numeric OR string variables, but not both. If both types of scalar are entered into a vector, the vector will automatically treat them as characters.

    f <- 1
ingredients <- c(a, b, c, d, e, f)

    '1' was input as a numeric character, but is now treated by R as a string.

    Using numeric values, you can also create vectors without having to directly type out every value. Using the colon operator, for example, you can create a list that counts by 1's from the first value to the second. This may increase if the second value is the highest or decrease if the second value is lower than the first. No matter what value you start with, the value will always increase or decrease by 1.

    ascend <- 1:5
descend <- 5.1:1.9

    In the second example above, we descend from 5.1 to 1.9. However, 1.9 is 3.2 steps away from 5.1, our final list does not include 1.9 as a value. Rather, it stops at the nearest number that is an interval of 1 away from the starting value.

    If you do not want to count in 1's, you can use the sequence function, seq(), to define specific intervals, using either “by = ” or “length.out =”. Defining “by = x” will specify the lengths of your intervals, so “by = 5” would count by fives from your starting value to your ending value, while “by = 2” would count by twos, etc. Conversely, “length.out = x” will specify the number of values you want in your final vector, and R will determine the lengths of the intervals.

    # Count from 1 to 5 in steps of 1 (same as above lists)
count <- seq(from = 1, to = 5, by = 1)

# Count from 1 to 5 in steps of 0.5
count <- seq(from = 1, to = 5, by = 0.5)

# Count from 1 to 5 and produce a list with a length of 3 numbers
count <- seq(from = 1, to = 5, length.out = 3)

    You can also generate a series of randomly selected numbers in a number of ways, from a number of different distributions. One of the most common methods is to draw from a normal distribution using rnorm(). To do this, you will first define n as the number of observations you would like to select, then define the mean and standard deviation of the distribution.

    scores <- rnorm(n = 5, mean = 100, sd = 15)

    However, since these numbers are selected RANDOMLY, their values will change every time the code is run. A simple way around this would be to set the seed, which essentially tells R which random series of numbers you are drawing your values from and ensures the values will be the same each time the code is run, as long as the seed is set.

    To do this, you can simply use set.seed() and select any number inside the brackets.

    set.seed(604)
scores <- rnorm(n = 5, mean = 100, sd = 15)

    While vectors are one-dimensional, matrices are two-dimensional, and probably look a lot more like most of the data you will be working with. Rather than a single row or column, matrices combine vectors into multiple rows and columns.

    This may be done by simply combining vectors as rows using rbind() or columns using cbind().

    # Define vectors
participants <- 1:5
age <- c(20, 20, 21, 22, 24)
iq <- rnorm(n = 5, mean = 100, sd = 15)

# Combine as columns
matrix <- cbind(participants, age, iq)

# Combine as rows
matrix <- rbind(participants, age, iq)

    This may also be done by creating a data frame, which also allows you to name your columns by variable.

    # Create a data frame from the above defined vectors
dataframe <- data.frame("id" = participants, "age" = age, "iq" = iq)

# Or you could put the values in directly rather than specifying on separate lines of code, though this may make the code messier and more difficult to read

dataframe <- data.frame("id" = 1:5, "age" = c(20, 20, 21, 22, 24), 
                        "iq" = rnorm(n = 5, mean = 100, sd = 15))

# NOTE: we set the seed earlier, so the values shouuld be the same for iq each time; however, were we to only run this sect of code, we would need to make sure to set the seed again

    Producing this data frame will likely produce data that is more similar to what you may be used to seeing.

    In general, you likely will not be generating data within R unless you are using it for something like a simulation study or for teaching purposes; and inputting data manually for large datasets is cumbersome and problematic. Most of the time, you will likely want to input datasets from other programs and read them as data frames into R to work with directly.

    Base R is capable of reading many types of data files, meaning no library installation is necessary to call upon your data. Common data file extensions include .txt, .xls, and .csv. The exact code you're going to use for this may change depending on data file type (e.g. you would use read.table() to call a .txt file, and read.csv to call a csv file). More information on that can be found here: https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/utils/versions/3.6.2/topics/read.table

    When inputting data files, you must first ensure your working directory is set to the location of the data file; otherwise, R will not be able to locate the file. This can be done using the setwd() function and typing in the full file location, or simply using a point and click from the top menu, clicking Session > Set Working Directory > Choose Directory. (You may also select “to source file location” but only if your R file is already saved to the same file folder as the data you are analyzing.) Once you select your directory, a line of code will appear in the console. I suggest copy/pasting this to the beginning of your code so that you will not need to set the working directory manually each time you open the file, but can just click 'run'.

    To check your working directory, you can also use getwd() to make sure your working directory is properly set.

    Once your working directory is set, you can use the read.table() function for your file type. The format is expressed below. However, since this is just an example of what the code would look like and does not call an actual file, it will currently produce only an error. Make sure your file name is in quotes and includes the file extension (.txt, .csv, etc.).

    Do not forget to specify the data to an object so that it can be called easily later.

    dat <- read.table("your file name.txt", header = T)

    ## Warning in file(file, "rt"): cannot open file 'your file name.txt': No such file or
## directory

    ## Error in file(file, "rt"): cannot open the connection

    # header = T implies that each column has been given a name in the file and the first line of every column is the column name. If this is not the case, remove this part of the code. This is not necessary to include when using the read.csv() function.

dat <- read.csv("your file name.csv")

    ## Warning in file(file, "rt"): cannot open file 'your file name.csv': No such file or
## directory

    ## Error in file(file, "rt"): cannot open the connection

    There are a number of extra options you can select when loading your data into R; however, you need not be too daunted by them, as generally you will just need to run code like the examples above to be on your way.

    Note that if you are loading SPSS, Stata, etc. files into R, you may need to install and activate the 'foreign' package first.

    install.packages("foreign")

    ## 
## The downloaded binary packages are in
##  /var/folders/82/msg9l88d7ss8xq30q1xlgypw0000gn/T//RtmpSFlsSm/downloaded_packages

    library(foreign)

dat <- read.spss("your file name.sav", to.data.frame = TRUE)

    ## Error in read.spss("your file name.sav", to.data.frame = TRUE): unable to open file: 'No such file or directory'

    Conditionals

    Conditional statements are used to test code or create nested coding branches. A condition must contain only one logical element: TRUE or FALSE.

    General Format: 

    if (logical_expression_1) {
expression_1
...
} else if (logical_expression_2) {
expression_2
...
} else {
expression_3
...
}

    Examples:

    # if 3 is greater than 2, print yes
if(3 > 2) print('yes')

    ## [1] "yes"

    # otherwise, do nothing
if(3 < 2) print('yes')

# if x is greater than y print yes, otherwise print no
y <- 10
x <- 5
if(x > y) print('yes') else print('no')

    ## [1] "no"

    An example of nested conditionals:

    if(x > y){
if(x == 2 * y) print('x is twice as large as y')
else print('x is larger than y')
} else if(x == y){
print('x and y are equal')
} else {
print('x is less than y')
}

    ## [1] "x is less than y"

    For Loops

    Loops are used to repeat tasks without re-copying the same code. For-loops, in particular, are finite and will eventually conclude after iteration over the chosen vector (e.g., 1:N).

    General Format:

    for(i in vector) {
expression_1
...
}

    Examples:

    for(i in 1:4){
x <- i * 5
cat(x, ' ')
}

    ## 5  10  15  20

    Application

    ## Confidence Interval for the mean difference

#Two independent samples example

scores <- c(19,9,21,27,33,20,24,14,26,21,28,15,26,
            21,20,22,18,25,15,19)
length(scores)

    ## [1] 20

    group <- rep(c("t","c"),each=10)
group

    ##  [1] "t" "t" "t" "t" "t" "t" "t" "t" "t" "t" "c" "c" "c" "c" "c" "c" "c" "c" "c" "c"

    #Mean Difference
mean(scores[group=="t"])-mean(scores[group=="c"])

    ## [1] 0.5

    #Percentile Based CI on the mean difference
nboot <- 1000
md <- numeric(nboot)

for (i in 1:nboot) {
  md[i] <- mean(sample(scores[group=="t"],length(scores[group=="t"]),replace=TRUE)) -
    mean(sample(scores[group=="c"],length(scores[group=="c"]),replace=TRUE))
}

CI95 <- quantile(md,probs=c(.025,.975))
CI95

    ##  2.5% 97.5% 
##  -4.4   5.3

    CI90 <- quantile(md,probs=c(.05,.95))
CI90

    ##     5%    95% 
## -3.605  4.600

    While Loops

    While loops, on the other hand, can be infinite unless stopped by a logical condition.

    General format:

    while (logical_expression) {
expression_1
...
}

    Example:

    y <- 0; x <- 1
while(x < 4){
x <- x - 1
print('No end in sight')
if(y == 2) break
y <- y + 1
}

    ## [1] "No end in sight"
## [1] "No end in sight"
## [1] "No end in sight"

    Built-in R Functions

    Everything we accomplish in R uses functions. Functions can import data, manipulate/clean our data, and export our data to use elsewhere. They are the fundamental building blocks within R.

    Here are a few examples of mathematical functions in R:

    sqrt(9)
exp(1)     # e^1
log(10)    # log function with base of e
log(10, base=exp(1))    # log function with base of e
log(10, base=10)        # log function with base of 10
factorial(3)            # 3!, factorial operator
pi                      # pie = 3.1415....
sqrt(2^2+5)             # Combination operation
(8+6)/(8-1)             # bracket

    Creating Functions

    General Format:

    myfunction <- function(arguments){
body_of_code
...
return_some_object
}

    example: 

    conversion <- function(radian){
radian * 180 / pi
}

conversion(pi)

    ## [1] 180

    conversion(pi/4)

    ## [1] 45

    Whatever is defined within a function does not affect definitions outside the function.

    example:

    myobj <- 'This is a string'
fun <- function(obj){
myobj <- 10 #masks the object outside temporarily
obj + myobj
}
fun(100)

    ## [1] 110

    So, you could have multiple objects with the same name as the object inside the function masks the object outside of it due to R’s scoping rules.

    However, there are some problematic scoping rules.

    example:

    myfun <- function(x) x + y * 2
y <- 10
myfun(20)

    ## [1] 40

    y <- 10
myfun(20)

    ## [1] 40

    This sort of behavior is not permitted in other programming languages. To avoid this problem, functions should be self-contained. That is, only objects visible within the function are used by using the correct arguments. 

    myfun2 <- function(x, y) x + y * 2
y <- 10
myfun2(20, y)

    ## [1] 40

    It's important to point out that functions can have default arguments; that is, arguments that remain constant unless otherwise overwritten.

    example

    myfun <- function(x, print = FALSE){
ret <- x^2
if(print) cat('The value is:', ret, '\n')
ret
}

myfun(10)

    ## [1] 100

    myfun(20, print = TRUE)

    ## The value is: 400

    ## [1] 400

    Functions within functions

    f <- function(x) x + 1
g <- function(y){
y2 <- y * 2
res <- f(y2)
res
}
g(10)

    ## [1] 21

    Functions can be passed as arguments as well.

    example:

    f <- function(x) x + 1
g <- function(y, fun){
y2 <- y * 2
res <- fun(y2) # notice the difference on this line
res
}
g(10, f)

    ## [1] 21

    For this section, we are going to be discussing how to calculate descriptive statistics in R, and have a basic overview of how to look at our data once we've imported everything.

    First, let's load in our data and activate our libraries. We're going to be using the mtcars dataset that comes built into R (saved here as an object called cars). We're also going to be installing and using the psych package.

    #install.packages("psych")
library(psych)

cars <- mtcars

    Now that we've got R set up and our data and libraries loaded, we can start by getting a quick look at the dataset to see what variables we have and what kind of data we're working with.

    # Get the names of columns
names(cars)

    ##  [1] "mpg"  "cyl"  "disp" "hp"   "drat" "wt"   "qsec" "vs"   "am"   "gear" "carb"

    # View the top few rows of the dataset
head(cars)

    ##                    mpg cyl disp  hp drat    wt  qsec vs am gear carb
## Mazda RX4         21.0   6  160 110 3.90 2.620 16.46  0  1    4    4
## Mazda RX4 Wag     21.0   6  160 110 3.90 2.875 17.02  0  1    4    4
## Datsun 710        22.8   4  108  93 3.85 2.320 18.61  1  1    4    1
## Hornet 4 Drive    21.4   6  258 110 3.08 3.215 19.44  1  0    3    1
## Hornet Sportabout 18.7   8  360 175 3.15 3.440 17.02  0  0    3    2
## Valiant           18.1   6  225 105 2.76 3.460 20.22  1  0    3    1

    You can also look at specific variables using the name of the dataframe object followed by the '$' operator and the name of the specific column you would like to inspect.

    # Look at just the mpg column
cars$mpg

    ##  [1] 21.0 21.0 22.8 21.4 18.7 18.1 14.3 24.4 22.8 19.2 17.8 16.4 17.3 15.2 10.4 10.4
## [17] 14.7 32.4 30.4 33.9 21.5 15.5 15.2 13.3 19.2 27.3 26.0 30.4 15.8 19.7 15.0 21.4

    This is particularly useful if you want to inspect the descriptives for only one or a subset of columns. So we could find the mean of a specific column by calling on the mean() and sd() functions and specifying the column we are interested in.

    # Find the mean and standard deviation of the mpg column
mean(cars$mpg)

    ## [1] 20.09062

    sd(cars$mpg)

    ## [1] 6.026948

    We can find most of the common descriptive statistics in base R, just by coding the function and specifying the specific column we want to summarize. Other common descriptives might be range(), median(), min(), max(), etc. (Note that base R's mode() function does not give the statistical mode; it tells you an object's storage type.)

    However, it can be incredibly cumbersome to analyze multiple variables using a line of code for each statistic. This dataset has 11 variables, so even to find the mean and standard deviation for each would require 22 lines of code without use of a simpler method. This method is most useful for quickly pulling specific stats from specific columns.

    If you want to describe your whole dataset, it would be a lot more efficient to use a single function. The 'describe' function in the psych package is one of the simplest ways to take care of this. 

    # Find all descriptives for the dataset
# By default, missing values will be removed. If you would like missing values to be included, you can add "na.rm = FALSE" to the code
# by specifying "digits =", we can also specify the number of digits following the decimal
describe(cars)

    ##      vars  n   mean     sd median trimmed    mad   min    max  range  skew kurtosis
## mpg     1 32  20.09   6.03  19.20   19.70   5.41 10.40  33.90  23.50  0.61    -0.37
## cyl     2 32   6.19   1.79   6.00    6.23   2.97  4.00   8.00   4.00 -0.17    -1.76
## disp    3 32 230.72 123.94 196.30  222.52 140.48 71.10 472.00 400.90  0.38    -1.21
## hp      4 32 146.69  68.56 123.00  141.19  77.10 52.00 335.00 283.00  0.73    -0.14
## drat    5 32   3.60   0.53   3.70    3.58   0.70  2.76   4.93   2.17  0.27    -0.71
## wt      6 32   3.22   0.98   3.33    3.15   0.77  1.51   5.42   3.91  0.42    -0.02
## qsec    7 32  17.85   1.79  17.71   17.83   1.42 14.50  22.90   8.40  0.37     0.34
## vs      8 32   0.44   0.50   0.00    0.42   0.00  0.00   1.00   1.00  0.24    -2.00
## am      9 32   0.41   0.50   0.00    0.38   0.00  0.00   1.00   1.00  0.36    -1.92
## gear   10 32   3.69   0.74   4.00    3.62   1.48  3.00   5.00   2.00  0.53    -1.07
## carb   11 32   2.81   1.62   2.00    2.65   1.48  1.00   8.00   7.00  1.05     1.26
##         se
## mpg   1.07
## cyl   0.32
## disp 21.91
## hp   12.12
## drat  0.09
## wt    0.17
## qsec  0.32
## vs    0.09
## am    0.09
## gear  0.13
## carb  0.29

    # This function will provide all of the most common descriptive statistics including mean, median, mode, standard deviation, etc. as well as skew and kurtosis to provide an idea of the shape of the distribution
# Negative skewness values indicate that the distribution is skewed to the left, while positive indicates skew to the right.
# Negative kurtosis indicates thin tails (platykurtic distributions), and positive values represent longer tails (leptokurtic distributions).
# You can also opt to exclude values of range and skew by adding "range = FALSE" and/or "skew = FALSE"

# For a more brief list of descriptives, you can add "fast = T", which will delete columns like skew, kurtosis, trimmed, etc.
# We will also use the "digits =" to set the number of digits we want after the decimal
describe(cars, fast = T)

    ##      vars  n   mean     sd   min    max  range    se
## mpg     1 32  20.09   6.03 10.40  33.90  23.50  1.07
## cyl     2 32   6.19   1.79  4.00   8.00   4.00  0.32
## disp    3 32 230.72 123.94 71.10 472.00 400.90 21.91
## hp      4 32 146.69  68.56 52.00 335.00 283.00 12.12
## drat    5 32   3.60   0.53  2.76   4.93   2.17  0.09
## wt      6 32   3.22   0.98  1.51   5.42   3.91  0.17
## qsec    7 32  17.85   1.79 14.50  22.90   8.40  0.32

    If your dataset includes a grouping variable, you can also find descriptives by group level. So in this dataset, the 'am' variable is coded as 0 or 1 to indicate the car has an automatic (0) or manual (1) transmission. This 'dummy coding' means that it can be used as a grouping variable. We can therefore look at the means of other variables between types of transmission.

    # Describe 'cars' dataset by type of transmission
describeBy(cars, group = 'am', digits = 2)

    As you can see from the output of the above code, we now have 2 sets of descriptive statistics, one for am: 0 and another for am: 1.

    Another common data inspection tool is graphs and distributions. There are numerous kinds of graphs, and some of these will be explored further using GGPlot; however, below, we will go over a few of the more common graph types.

    To build off of our investigation of descriptive statistics, we may wish to generate a frequency distribution such as a histogram (continuous data) or bar graph (categorical data). This can be done easily in base R without installing any new packages. In this case, we will be using the mpg variable as an example of continuous data, and cyl as an example of categorical/discrete data. 

    # Creating a basic histogram for continuous variables
# Titles are optional, but improve readability
hist(cars$mpg, xlab = "Miles Per Gallon", ylab = "Frequency", main = "MPG Frequency Distribution")


    # Create a bar plot for discrete variables
# table() counts how many cars have each number of cylinders
barplot(table(cars$cyl), xlab = "Cylinders", ylab = "Frequency", main = "Cylinders Frequency Distribution")

    If you wish to create a stacked or grouped bar plot, you may define the variables you want to graph and call upon the table object in your code.

    # Create a stacked barplot
stackedvars <- table(cars$am, cars$cyl)
barplot(stackedvars, xlab = "Number of Cylinders", ylab = "Frequency", main = "Frequency Distribution of Cylinders by Transmission", col = c("blue", "green"), legend = rownames(stackedvars))


    # "col =" will define the colours you wish to use
# "legend =" will create a legend so that it is clear which variable corresponds to each colour

# Side by Side
# Add "beside = T" to the above code
barplot(stackedvars, xlab = "Number of Cylinders", ylab = "Frequency", main = "Frequency Distribution of Cylinders by Transmission", col = c("blue", "green"), legend = rownames(stackedvars), beside = T)

    Of course, other customizations are also possible, which we do not have the time to go through directly here. However, you can look up either the “hist” or “barplot” functions to see more possible additions. You can also adjust the placement of your figure on the plot using the par() function (https://www.datamentor.io/r-programming/subplot/).

    Say we want to visually inspect the relationship between miles per gallon and weight of a vehicle. Simple scatterplots are also relatively easily created in base R using the 'plot' function. This can similarly be customized for aspects like colour and placement, but we will be focusing here on a basic introduction to plotting functions.

    Using the plot function, we will first input the variable to plot on the x-axis, then the variable we want on the y-axis. We should also add in titles for interpretability.

    # Generate basic scatterplot of miles per gallon by weight
plot(cars$wt, cars$mpg, xlab = "Weight", ylab = "Miles per Gallon", main = "Miles per Gallon by Weight")
# Add a line of best fit (linear)
abline(lm(mpg ~ wt, data = cars), col = "blue")
# Add a lowess line
lines(lowess(cars$wt, cars$mpg), col = "red")

    It is important to note that in order to create scatterplots, you must have equal numbers of cases between x and y. If there are missing values in either categories, you will need to remove missing values. This can be done using “complete.cases”. Although unnecessary for this dataset, the code would look like this:

    # Create another data object that has only complete cases of every variable
cars.complete <- cars[complete.cases(cars),]

    When doing this, I would suggest creating a new dataframe object, like “cars.complete” so that the original data frame and its information isn't lost or deleted.

    You may also be interested in inspecting quickly the correlations between variables to see if any relationship appears to exist or to quickly eyeball the data for linearity (although this should be examined much more in depth through other testing - this method will only indicate major violations).

    To do this simply for all variables at once, we can install a package called GGally and use the 'ggpairs' function as follows. (You can do this in Base R, too, using plot(x) where 'x' is your data object. However, the output is extremely messy and difficult to read, particularly when you have many variables.)

    # Install GGally
#install.packages("GGally")

# Load library
#library(GGally)

# Inspect correlations
#ggpairs(cars, diag = list(continuous = "barDiag"))

    These graphs aren't the prettiest but they will give you some indication of what variables might be related, which can be useful for procedures such as selecting what variables to include in a multiple regression.

    Data Manipulation

    Several categorical variables (e.g., am -> transmission type, cyl -> # of cylinders) should be coded as factors to indicate that they are not really quantitative variables but rather numerical representations of categorical variables.

    mtcars <- within(mtcars, {
  fvs <- factor(vs, levels=c(0,1), labels = c('V-engine', 'Straight-engine'))
  fam <- factor(am, levels=c(0,1), labels = c('automatic', 'manual'))
  fcyl <- factor(cyl) # levels here are fine as-is
})

    #Subsetting (i.e., keeping) certain data

#Say we're only interested in conducting an analysis on the number of cylinders (cyl) and Miles/gallon (mpg)
myvars <- c("mpg", "cyl")
analyse <- mtcars[myvars]

#Or say that you want to delete only those two variables from the dataset
analyse <- mtcars[,-c(1,2)]

#Use subset() to select data dependent on other variables
#E.g., Say you only want to inspect data pertaining to automatic automobiles with V-shaped engines
analyse <- subset(mtcars, fvs == 'V-engine' & fam == 'automatic')

#A step further: mpg pertaining to the labels 'V-engine' and 'automatic'
analyse <- subset(mtcars, fvs == 'V-engine' & fam == 'automatic', select=c(mpg, fvs, fam))

    #wide vs long dataframes

#example 1: using gather()

#wide format:
before<-rnorm(n=100,mean=0.1)
after<-rnorm(n=100,mean=0.5)
wide_data<-data.frame(before,after)

#let's convert it to long format

long_data <- gather(wide_data, occurrence, scores, before, after, factor_key=TRUE)

#example 2: using reshape2()
#wide format:
wide_data <- data.frame(id = factor(1:4), time1 = rlnorm(4), 
                        time2 = rlnorm(4)+4, time3 = rlnorm(4)+8, 
                        time4 = rlnorm(4)+12)
#factor(1:5) creates the number of observations (4 in this case)
#4 variables: time 1, time 2, time 3, time 4
#rlnorm(4) retrieves 4 values from a log-normal distribution (i.e., only positive #s)

long_data <- melt(wide_data, id.vars='id', 
               value.name = 'scores', variable.name = 'time')

sigma_2 <- 2

# generate data

               id = rep(x=c(1:n_1),
                        times = c(2)

#wide-format

# - data: Data object

data_wide <- spread(data = data_long, key = group, value =score)
#or

data_wide <- dcast(data_long, id ~ group, value.var="score")

#deleting observations 
data_long <- data_long[-c(4, 8, 15), ]

    Statistical Analyses

    #Independent t-tests
mtcars <- within(mtcars, {
  fvs <- factor(vs, levels=c(0,1), labels = c('V-engine', 'Straight-engine'))
  fam <- factor(am, levels=c(0,1), labels = c('automatic', 'manual'))
  fcyl <- factor(cyl) # levels here are fine as-is
})

#Is an automatic or manual transmission better for mpg? (independent samples t-test)

x <- subset(mtcars,fam == 'automatic', select=c(mpg))
y <- subset(mtcars,fam == 'manual', select=c(mpg))

#box plot
ggplot(mtcars, aes(fam, mpg)) + geom_boxplot()

qqnorm(x$mpg, main='automatic')

res

    #One-way ANOVA
#let's say we're interested in investigating the relationship between three teaching methods (a 3-level factor variable)
#and test scores. 
#generate data
n_3<- 70
mu_3<-50
sigma_3<-2

data_long <- tibble(
  id = rep(x=c(1:n_1),
           times = c(3)
  ),

  group = rep(x = c("method.1","method.2", "method.3"),
              times = c(n_1,n_2, n_3)),

  score = c(rnorm(n = n_1,
                  mean = mu_1,
                  sd = sigma_1),
            rnorm(n = n_2,
                  mean = mu_2,
                  sd = sigma_2),
            rnorm(n = n_3,
                  mean = mu_3,
                  sd = sigma_3)
            )
)

#convert it to a wide format 
data_wide <- spread(data = data_long, key = group, value =score)

#boxplot
ggplot(data_long, aes(group, score)) + geom_boxplot()


    #assumptions we can test in R:
#normality (i.e., the outcome variable is normally distributed in each of the factor levels)
#homogeneity of variance (HOV) (i.e., the variances of the outcome variable are equal across the factor levels)

#checking the normality assumption:
qqnorm(data_wide$method.1)
qqline(data_wide$method.1)


    qqnorm(data_wide$method.2)
qqline(data_wide$method.2)


    qqnorm(data_wide$method.3)
qqline(data_wide$method.3)


    #run Levene's test to check assumption of homogeneity of variance
#by default centres variable using median 
leveneTest(score~group, data=data_long,center=mean)

    ## Warning in leveneTest.default(y = y, group = group, ...): group coerced to factor.

    ## Levene's Test for Homogeneity of Variance (center = mean)
##        Df F value Pr(>F)
## group   2  0.9292 0.3965
##       207

    #p>.05 therefore assumption met 

#running one-way ANOVA 
model<-aov(score~group, data=data_long)
summary(model)

    ##              Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)    
## group         2  33064   16532    3681 <2e-16 ***
## Residuals   207    930       4                   
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

    #calculating effect size
#typically eta-squared is reported, but omega squared is less biased
omega_squared(model)

    ## For one-way between subjects designs, partial omega squared is equvilant to omega squared.
## Returning omega squared.

    ## Parameter | Omega2 |       90% CI
## ---------------------------------
## group     |   0.97 | [0.97, 0.98]

    eta_squared(model, ci=0.95)

    ## For one-way between subjects designs, partial eta squared is equvilant to eta squared.
## Returning eta squared.

    ## Parameter | Eta2 |       95% CI
## -------------------------------
## group     | 0.97 | [0.97, 0.98]

    #Since the F-ratio was significant, then at least one group mean is different
#To determine which pairs of groups are different, you can run a post-hoc test

#Post hoc analyses
#Tukey HSD
TukeyHSD(model)

    ##   Tukey multiple comparisons of means
##     95% family-wise confidence level
## 
## Fit: aov(formula = score ~ group, data = data_long)
## 
## $group
##                        diff       lwr      upr p adj
## method.2-method.1  9.540364  8.694676 10.38605     0
## method.3-method.1 30.073269 29.227582 30.91896     0
## method.3-method.2 20.532906 19.687218 21.37859     0

    #HOV not met?
#run one-way ANOVA using oneway.test 
oneway.test(score~group, data=data_long, var=F) #if HOV not met be sure to include var=F

    ## 
##  One-way analysis of means (not assuming equal variances)
## 
## data:  score and group
## F = 3483.3, num df = 2.0, denom df = 137.7, p-value < 2.2e-16

    #Rather than Tukey HSD, Games-Howell is used as a post-hoc test 
#Since it is based on Welch’s correction to the degrees of freedom
games_howell_test(data_long, score~group)

    ## # A tibble: 3 x 8

    #Two-way ANOVA

#generate data
n_3<- 70
mu_3<-50
sigma_3<-2
factor2<-sample(c("F","M"),n_1, replace = T)

data_long <- tibble(
  id = rep(x=c(1:n_1),

                  mean = mu_3,

)

#convert it to a wide format 
data_wide <- spread(data_long, method, score)


#Generate a crosstab to ensure you have observations in each group
table(data_long$method, data_long$sex)

Summarize(score~ method +sex, data=data_long, digits=2)

    #If assumptions (e.g., normality) are not met, a common non-parametric alternative is the Kruskal-Wallis test
#(for a two-way design like this one, its extension is the Scheirer-Ray-Hare test, computed below)
#Rank your outcome variable 
data_long$rankScore<-rank(data_long$score)

#Run regular ANOVA using aov function to get SS and df values
KW<-aov(rankScore~method*sex, data=data_long)
summary(KW)

    ##              Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)    
## method        2 685860  342930 847.933 <2e-16 ***
## sex           1    350     350   0.865 0.3535    
## method:sex    2   3019    1509   3.732 0.0256 *  
## Residuals   204  82504     404                   
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

    #Extract the sums of squares and df values then compute the sum for each
Df=anova(KW)[,"Df"]
SS=anova(KW)[,"Sum Sq"]
Sum_df=sum(Df)
Sum_SS=sum(SS)

#Compute the total mean square value
MS=Sum_SS/Sum_df

#Computing H values and associated p value for the main effects and interaction
Hmethod=SS[1]/MS
1-pchisq(Hmethod,Df[1])

    ## [1] 0

    Hsex=SS[2]/MS
1-pchisq(Hsex,Df[2])

    ## [1] 0.7582742

    Hinteraction=SS[3]/MS
1-pchisq(Hinteraction,Df[3])

    ## [1] 0.6644522

    Progress in Module 3

    Correlation and Regression

    For this section, we will be discussing correlation and regression using base R (and plots from GGally). As with all things in R, there are multiple ways of doing this. However, for simple regression and first level multiple regression - particularly for linear relationships - base R has everything you need.

    First, let's load in our data, using the mtcars dataset once more.

    data(mtcars)

    In previous weeks, you were shown how to generate graphs and correlations using ggpairs. This is a good practice when beginning a regression to take a quick look at the relationships between variables.

    # Load GGally library
library(GGally)

# Investigate pairs
ggpairs(mtcars, diag = list(continuous = "barDiag"), title = "Correlations between variables in mtcars")

    If we look at the graph here, we can see that there appear to be some relationships that are quite strong in either direction. The asterisks next to some of these correlations indicate statistical significance (* = p < .05, ** = p < .01, *** = p < .001), and we can see that many of these relationships are highly significant.

    Also, note that some variables like cylinders appear to have straight lines at each of their data points. This is because they are categorical variables, so there is no possible values in between those points, so do not be alarmed by this output. It is to be expected.

    Say we are interested only in one or two of the relationships here, rather than all. We can also investigate individual relationships between variables using cor() or cor.test() to test for significance.

    # Investigate the correlation between miles per gallon and weight
cor(mtcars$mpg, mtcars$wt)

    ## [1] -0.8676594

    # The correlation comes out to be approximately -.87, which is pretty strong. We would expect this to be statistically significant given its magnitude, but if we want to know the exact p-value or we were to test variables with a weaker relationship, we might instead opt to use a proper hypothesis test.

# Investigate the correlation using cor.test
cor.test(mtcars$mpg, mtcars$wt)

    ## 
##  Pearson's product-moment correlation
## 
## data:  mtcars$mpg and mtcars$wt
## t = -9.559, df = 30, p-value = 1.294e-10
## alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  -0.9338264 -0.7440872
## sample estimates:
##        cor 
## -0.8676594

    # Now we can see that the p-value is 1.294*10^-10, or p < .001. The relationship is highly significant. 
# Another benefit to cor.test is that it can produce a confidence interval, in this case: 95% CI[-.93, -.74].

    There are multiple variants of correlations we can investigate. By default, these functions look at the Pearson's product moment coefficient (r), which describes the linear relationship between two variables. However, not all relationships are well represented by Pearson's r. You can modify the code to instead obtain an estimate using Spearman's rho or Kendall's tau if the samples do not come from a bivariate normal distribution.

    # Test the relationship between horsepower and cylinders
cor.test(mtcars$hp, mtcars$cyl)

    ## 
##  Pearson's product-moment correlation
## 
## data:  mtcars$hp and mtcars$cyl
## t = 8.2286, df = 30, p-value = 3.478e-09
## alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  0.6816016 0.9154223
## sample estimates:
##       cor 
## 0.8324475

    # Test the relationship between horsepower and cylinders using Spearman's rho
cor.test(mtcars$hp, mtcars$cyl, method = "spearman")

    ## Warning in cor.test.default(mtcars$hp, mtcars$cyl, method = "spearman"): Cannot compute
## exact p-value with ties

    ## 
##  Spearman's rank correlation rho
## 
## data:  mtcars$hp and mtcars$cyl
## S = 535.83, p-value = 1.868e-12
## alternative hypothesis: true rho is not equal to 0
## sample estimates:
##       rho 
## 0.9017909

    # Note how the relationship appears to have changed due to better estimation procedure

    Now, we can get to simple linear regression; that is, regression with a single predictor that is linearly related to the outcome variable. Let's say miles per gallon is our dependent variable and we are interested in whether it can be significantly predicted by horsepower. To do this, we would use the lm() function and define the equation as “y ~ x”, meaning “y” is predicted by “x”. Then, we can use the summary() function to investigate the parameters and fit of our model.

    # Simple linear regression
simplemod <- lm(mpg ~ hp, data = mtcars)
summary(simplemod)

    ## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = mpg ~ hp, data = mtcars)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -5.7121 -2.1122 -0.8854  1.5819  8.2360 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept) 30.09886    1.63392  18.421  < 2e-16 ***
## hp          -0.06823    0.01012  -6.742 1.79e-07 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 3.863 on 30 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.6024, Adjusted R-squared:  0.5892 
## F-statistic: 45.46 on 1 and 30 DF,  p-value: 1.788e-07

    # Here we can look at the residuals and p-values, as well as R-squared and adjusted R-squared. Interpreting residuals is highly dependent on the range and scale of your own data, but we can see that R-squared is .6024. This value represents the estimated proportion of variance in mpg that is predicted by hp. That is, about 60%, indicating a strong relationship.
# The estimate of the intercept represents the value of the predicted value of the dependent variable when the predictor variable = 0
# The estimate of the slope of the predictor is shown next to 'hp'. In this case, we can interpret this such that for every one point increase in horsepower, we would expect miles per gallon to decrease by approximately 0.07.
# We can also see that this relationship is statistically significant (p < .001).

    We can also test the assumptions of the model by using the plot() function, which will bring up four different graphs to let us inspect linearity, homogeneity of variance, extreme values, and normality. You will be prompted to hit return to bring up each successive plot but you can scroll back and forth through them.

    # Test assumptions
plot(simplemod)

    For plot 1, “residuals vs. fitted”, you'll want to look at the shape of the red line to investigate linearity. In general, we want this line to be relatively straight along the 0 axis. Now, this line is very misshapen and may be indicative of a violation of linearity. However, we have very few observations (n = 32), and these spaces where the line deviates seems to be affected by only a handful of observations that are further out, so it's difficult to ascertain the degree to which this relationship has violated linearity but this indicates we may want to investigate further and perhaps try removing observations and testing for differences, or attempting quadratic relationships. The latter goes beyond the scope of this course.

    We can also use this plot to investigate homogeneity of variance, for which we would like to see the points on the graph create something of a cloudlike shape. Otherwise, there may be issues with violation of variance assumptions, which primarily affects statistical significance testing. Our biggest concern would be if the residuals formed a clear pattern or if there is a fan effect happening such that there are small residuals on one side and large residuals on the other. In this case, we can sort of see a pattern emerging that's somewhat quadratic in shape, but given the limited observations and only a small number on the edges, we may be fine.

    The second plot is a normal QQ plot, which you would assess by how close the observations fall on the line of the plot. Our data looks relatively normal. A few observations deviate up at the top right but it's likely not much cause for concern.

    The third plot is analyzed similarly to the first plot - for relative horizontal line shape and spread of residuals. This plot looks pretty good.

    Finally, the residuals vs. leverage plot can help you to identify outliers which may be skewing the estimates. We can see here Maserati Bora appears to be a potential outlier with a high Cook's Distance out here past 1. As such, it might be worth rerunning the model without that point to see how it may differ. The argument for keeping vs. removing outliers is still controversial in statistics, but an exploratory analysis to see how the model changes and reporting both may be worthwhile.

    If we have a categorical variable as our predictor, our output will look different in a simple regression. The intercept will represent the value of y at the first level of x, and each slope will represent the predicted difference in y between the first level of x and each that level of y.

    # First define cylinders as a factor, rather than a continuous variable
mtcars$cyl <- as.factor(mtcars$cyl)

# Check structure
str(mtcars$cyl)

    ##  Factor w/ 3 levels "4","6","8": 2 2 1 2 3 2 3 1 1 2 ...

    # Regression with categorical variables
catmod <- lm(mpg ~ cyl, data = mtcars)
summary(catmod)

    ## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = mpg ~ cyl, data = mtcars)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -5.2636 -1.8357  0.0286  1.3893  7.2364 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)  26.6636     0.9718  27.437  < 2e-16 ***
## cyl6         -6.9208     1.5583  -4.441 0.000119 ***
## cyl8        -11.5636     1.2986  -8.905 8.57e-10 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 3.223 on 29 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.7325, Adjusted R-squared:  0.714 
## F-statistic:  39.7 on 2 and 29 DF,  p-value: 4.979e-09

    # Now the intercept represents the predicted mpg given cylinders = 4
# cyl6 represents the expected change in mpg from cyl = 4 to cyl = 6
# cyl8 represents the expected change in mpg from cyl = 4 to cyl = 8

    Now that we have looked at simple regression, we can also take a quick look at estimating multiple regression models, or models with multiple predictors.

    We can use the same lm() function to account for multiple predictors by adding the + sign between each predictor variable on the right side of the tilde (“~”). This will not include interaction effects unless specifically specified. Interaction effects are incorporated using multiplication (i.e. x1*x2). The interaction effect may be included as another predictor in a string of additive variables, or you can specify just the interaction, which will automatically test individual predictors as well.

    # Multiple regression (no interaction effects) predicting mpg from hp and weight
additive <- lm(mpg ~ hp + wt, data = mtcars)
summary(additive)

    ## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = mpg ~ hp + wt, data = mtcars)
## 
## Residuals:
##    Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
## -3.941 -1.600 -0.182  1.050  5.854 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept) 37.22727    1.59879  23.285  < 2e-16 ***
## hp          -0.03177    0.00903  -3.519  0.00145 ** 
## wt          -3.87783    0.63273  -6.129 1.12e-06 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 2.593 on 29 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.8268, Adjusted R-squared:  0.8148 
## F-statistic: 69.21 on 2 and 29 DF,  p-value: 9.109e-12

    # Now we have 2 slopes, one for horsepower and one for weight.
# With multiple regression, we should look at adjusted R-squared as opposed to multiple R-squared, because it adjusts for the number of predictors. In this case, the values are not very different and the model seems to improved to account for approximately 82% of the variance. 

# Multiple regression (with interaction)
multiplereg <- lm(mpg ~ hp + wt + hp*wt, data = mtcars) # OR, equivalently
multiplereg <- lm(mpg ~ hp*wt, data = mtcars)
summary(multiplereg)

    ## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = mpg ~ hp * wt, data = mtcars)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -3.0632 -1.6491 -0.7362  1.4211  4.5513 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept) 49.80842    3.60516  13.816 5.01e-14 ***
## hp          -0.12010    0.02470  -4.863 4.04e-05 ***
## wt          -8.21662    1.26971  -6.471 5.20e-07 ***
## hp:wt        0.02785    0.00742   3.753 0.000811 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 2.153 on 28 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.8848, Adjusted R-squared:  0.8724 
## F-statistic: 71.66 on 3 and 28 DF,  p-value: 2.981e-13

    In the above case, hp by wt is a significant interaction effect (p < .001), but our adjusted R-square only increased by .05. If we want to see if the more complex model is significantly better than the simpler model, we can use the anova() function and put both model names inside. A significant result will indicate that there is significant improvement to the model with the inclusion of the interaction.

    # Test for model improvement
anova(additive, multiplereg)

    ## Analysis of Variance Table
## 
## Model 1: mpg ~ hp + wt
## Model 2: mpg ~ hp * wt
##   Res.Df    RSS Df Sum of Sq      F    Pr(>F)    
## 1     29 195.05                                  
## 2     28 129.76  1    65.286 14.088 0.0008108 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

    # We can now justify selecting the model with the interaction effect included

    Data Wrangling skills are important to ensure that you have data in a “tidy” format.

    Tidy data ensures that your data are in the format that allows you to properly create graphs or run statistical analyses in R.

    Overview

    We will be learning how to use the dplyr package (part of tidyverse) to find different ways to present and transform our data.

    Main Functions

    select()

    relocate()

    filter()

    arrange()

    mutate()

    summarise()

    group_by()

    Packages

    #library(tidyverse)
#library(haven)
#library(babynames)
#library(dslabs)

    Data

    murders
head(murders)
describe(babynames)

df <- murders

    arrange()

    Sorting in ascending or descending order is pretty straightforward

    arrange(df, total) # sort on total from lowest to highest
arrange(df, desc(total)) # sort on total from highest to lowest

# here is the same code using the pipe instead

df %>%
    arrange(total)

df %>%
    arrange(desc(total))

    Note that while the output was sorted on total in any of these situations above, it does not change the sorting in your original dataset!

    Why?

    Remember that R is object based, and we did not create a new object that saves the sorting.

    To preserve the sorting in our dataset we have to either over-ride our df dataset or create a second version of our df dataset. E.g., 

    df2 <- df %>%
    arrange(total)
df2

    With arrange, saving a new dataset is trivial because there will be no effects on your statistics, but it is non-trivial if you start filtering and transforming variables, and then want to use this transformed dataset in an analysis.

    Note you can also sort across multiple variables. Note that the order matters because it sorts on the first variable first, then the next one, then the next one…etc.

    df %>% 
    arrange(total,population) # sort on total first, then on population (both lowest to highest)

df %>%
    arrange(total,desc(population))

    select()

    This function helps you work with a smaller version of your dataset (on the variable side). This can save you time so you don't have to scroll through to find the exact names of your variables (remember R is case sensitive so it has to be a perfect match).

    Our dataset has a small number of variables so it is already manageable but we will still see how to use the select function.

    NOTE: There is one really annoying issue with select() that may come up for you. select() is also the name of a function from the MASS package and MASS is loaded by default so R often wants to use that function instead.

    If you use ?select you will see it come up for two packages

    There are two ways you can fix this:

    sub.df <-  df %>%
    dplyr::select(abb, total) # tells R to use the select function from dplyr in this case only

select<-dplyr::select # tells R that you want to use the select function from dplyr EVERY time within this R session. If you close R, you will need to run this again

df %>%
    select(abb, total)

# other ways to use select

sub.df <- df %>% 
    select(-state) # all variables EXCEPT these ones

sub.df

df %>%
    select(region:total) # select everything starting in between region and total (inclusive)

# note if you want to use excluding a range you need parentheses around the variables with a minus sign in front of it
df %>%
    select(-(region:total)) # select everything excluding variables in between region and total (inclusive)

    filter()

    filter() allows you to work with a smaller number of rows in your dataset based on a communality. You can also think of this as subsetting your data to include participants with particular characteristics.

    Here is where you will be using logical data because you need to tell filter() not just the variable you want to filter on, but also the particular conditions or values.

    Here are some examples:

    df$state <- factor(df$state)
df$abb <- factor(df$abb)

# only west region

df %>%
    filter(region == "West")  # note that you need two equal signs

# at or more than 50 murders 

df %>%
    filter(total >= 50) # greater than or equal to

# population smaller than 1M

df %>%
    filter(population < 1000000) # less than 1M (doesn't include exactly 1M)

    You can also filter on multiple conditions

    # Only Northeast AND have more than 100 murders
df %>%
    filter(region == "Northeast" & total > 100)  # both of these have to be true

# West OR fewer than 100 murders

df %>%
    filter(region == "West" | total < 100) # only one of these needs to be true

# you could also say what you do NOT want

df %>%
    filter(region != "South") # != means not equal to

    Revisiting the dplyr 'pipeline'

    One of the convenient features of dplyr is that the functions and code were designed to be used together for limitless opportunities to analyze different versions of the dataset. You may not need to use some of the more advanced features but you will likely need to string at least a couple of them together at some point.

    In SPSS, you simply click through the different buttons and apply each of them separately to get all of your conditions applied.

    In R, you set up a “pipeline” using the symbol %>% as the pipe that joins everything together. You can think read this symbol as the word “then”

    Here's an example pipeline in plain English:

    Start with the df dataset and then Create a smaller subset of the dataset for only the variables state, abb, region, total and then Filter the dataset to only include West regions and then Sort the dataset by total from highest to lowest

    In R this would look like:

    df %>%
    select(state, abb, region, total) %>%
    filter(region == "West") %>%
    arrange(desc(total))

    Now we can easily find the highest (highest two, three, etc.) number of murders for west regions

    mutate()

    mutate() is used when you want to create a new variable in your dataset.

    For example, we may want to create a new murder ratio variable that is the total / population

    new_df<-df %>%
    mutate(murderatio =total/population)

new_df

new_df <- new_df %>%
  mutate(murderatio_percent = murderatio*100)

new_df

    You can also apply square root, log, etc. transformations to variables and apply mutate multiple variables in one step.

    summarise() and group_by()

    summarise() is most often used to get descriptive statistics at the end of the pipeline for particular subgroups, aggregates of groups, frequency counts, etc.

    How summarise() differs from output from regular summary statistics from functions like summary(), describe(), etc. is that the output itself is also a tibble that you could use in future analysis.

    Generally speaking, where I would find it more useful is if you need to use a series of data manipulation functions in the pipeline to get exploratory statistics for different groups or want to check something quickly.

    You can use it for general descriptive statistics if you want very specific pieces of information as well (especially used in conjunction with group_by() )

    You can find a list of useful functions to use in summarise here: https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/summarise.html 

    df %>%
    summarise(mean_cases=mean(total, na.rm=TRUE))


# with group_by

new_df %>%
    group_by(state) %>%
    summarise(mean_percent=mean(murderatio_percent, na.rm=TRUE))

new_df %>%
    group_by(region) %>%
    summarise(N=n())

    relocate()

    relocate allows you to change the position of some of your variables (move to front, end, before or after certain other variables, etc.)

    Changing variable order doesn't affect your analyses or statistics in any way but it may make things more convenient or neater for you. 

    # move a variable to front of data set (default action)

df2<-df %>%
    relocate(total)
df2

# move multiple variables to the front of data set

df2<-df %>%
    relocate(total, population)
df2

df
# move variable to a particular location

# total between abb and region

df3<- df %>%
    relocate(total, .before=region)

df3

    plotly

    library(plotly)

fig <- plot_ly(new_df, x = ~population, y = ~total, text = ~state, type = 'scatter', mode = 'markers', color = ~abb,
        marker = list(size = ~murderatio_percent*5000, opacity = 0.5))
fig <- fig %>% layout(title = 'Murders vs. Population by State',
         xaxis = list(showgrid = FALSE),
         yaxis = list(showgrid = FALSE))

fig



new_df %>%
  arrange(desc(murderatio_percent))

    #The R Markdown file is located here: https://rpubs.com/naomimg/markdownintro


    The following should be put inside the Shiny app R file:

    #Shiny is an R Package that allows you to create interactive web apps that you can deploy for anyone to use
#What makes Shiny different from other R packages that allow for user interactivity is reactivity and the ability to save user data
#R Scripts use imperative programming: you issue a specific command and it’s carried out immediately. That is, you command R to load your data, transform it, visualise it, and save the results to disk.
#Shiny uses declarative programming: you express higher-level goals or describe important constraints, and rely on someone else to decide how and/or when to translate that into action. 
#free (!) great resource: https://mastering-shiny.org/index.html
#The only downside to the book is that it doesn't include include information on how to save data remotely (which is, arguably, the most complicated part about Shiny)

#A Shiny app consists of the UI (user interface) and server 
library(ggplot2)
library(shiny)
library(shinyjs)
#shinyjs is a great package that includes functions that use javascript so that you don't have to figure out how to incorporate it in your app
#more info on shinyjs: https://deanattali.com/shinyjs/overview
colour.name <- c("","purple", "blue", "yellow", "I have no favourite colour")
#The UI is where you include code that generates output that you want the user to /see/
ui <- fluidPage(
useShinyjs(),
    # Application title
    titlePanel("Title"),

    # Sidebar with a slider input for number of bins 
    sidebarLayout(
        sidebarPanel(
        #input functions allow the user to input information
        #text inputs:
            textInput("name", "What's your name?"),
        #numeric inputs
            numericInput("number", "Choose a number", value = 0, min = 0, max = 100),
            sliderInput("slider", "This is a slider", value = 50, min = 0, max = 100), 
        #choose from a list
        selectInput("state", "What's your favourite colour?", colour.name),
        #File uploads
        fileInput("upload", NULL),
        #to save the user inputs, you'll need to use action buttons 
        actionButton("click", "Done"),
        #an action button isn't just for saving user data - you can use action buttons to let users switch from one task to another, start a new task, etc
        actionButton("button", "Hidden Button")
        ),

        # Show a plot of the generated distribution
        mainPanel(
            plotOutput("plot", brush = "plot_brush"),
            tableOutput("data"),
            textOutput("greeting")
        )
    )
)

# The server is where you include code that runs in the background (i.e., that the user cannot see)
server <- function(input, output) {
    output$plot <- renderPlot({
        ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) + geom_point()
    }, res = 96)

    output$data <- renderTable({
        brushedPoints(mtcars, input$plot_brush)
    })

    #example of reactivity: you’ll see that the greeting updates automatically as you type
    #you don’t need to tell an output when to update, because Shiny automatically figures it out for you
    output$greeting <- renderText({
        paste0("Hello ", input$name, "!")
    })

    observe(
        shinyjs::hide("button")
    )

    observeEvent(input$click, {shinyjs::show("button")})
}

# Run the application 
shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)

    Confirmatory Factor Analysis

    Structural equation modeling and factor analysis are big topics, and going over everything would take multiple courses, so today we're just going to quickly go over confirmatory factor analysis and how to code for specific types of models. For this, we will be using a dataset from a GRIT survey collected by Duckworth and Quinn (2009). We will be using the lavaan, lavaanPlot, and semPlot packages.

    # Load libraries
#library(lavaan)
#library(lavaanPlot)
#library(semPlot) # semPaths() comes from the semPlot package

# Load dataset
grit <- read.csv("Grit_Columns.csv")

    “Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) technique used to verify the factor structure of a set of observed variables. CFA allows the researcher to test the hypothesis that a relationship between observed variables and their underlying latent construct(s) exists. The researcher uses knowledge of the theory, empirical research, or both, postulates the relationship pattern a priori, and then tests the hypothesis statistically.” - Suhr (2006 - from https://support.sas.com/resources/papers/proceedings/proceedings/sugi31/200-31.pdf)

    We will not be going into the statistical techniques behind CFAs here, but will provide an overview of how to code for CFAs and interpret the output from R. The models we will be producing here will be one-factor, two-factor (correlated factors), and bifactor models, with a brief look at higher-order models.

    Given that a CFA requires hypothesized models of how items interact with latent constructs, we must first have an idea of what our scale's model should be in order to use it. In the absence of this, we would be using exploratory factor analysis to estimate the best fitting model that can be explained by theory.

    Starting with the one-factor model, we will first specify how all items in the dataset relate, then use the cfa() function in the lavaan library to fit the model to the data, and finally use the summary() function to read the output. In the summary line, we also have to specify if we want to get fit measures and standardized estimates.

    One-Factor Model

    The short version GRIT includes 8 items with scores ranging from 1 to 5. Items 2, 4, 7, and 8 are reverse-coded. We want to assign all items to a single factor. To assign items to a factor, we use the structure 'factorname =~ item1 + item2 + item3…' where factorname is whatever you choose to call your factor and item1, item2, etc. are whatever the items of your dataset are titled. We can also specify correlated errors by using double tildes (~~) such that it would appear as “item1 ~~ item2”.

    # Specify the model
onefactormod <- 'factor =~ GS2 + GS4 + GS5 + GS6 + GS7 + GS8 + GS9 + GS12'
onefactor <- cfa(onefactormod, data = grit)
summary(onefactor, fit.measures = T, standardized = T)
# "fit.measures = T" will give you the fit measures like CFI, TLI, RMSEA, and SRMR at the beginning of the output
# "standardized = T" will give you standardized estimates in the std.all column on the right of the estimates columns

    If we scroll to the top of our model output, we can see all of the fit statistics, which show a weak model fit. Although, due to high sample size, the significant chi-square value is to be expected, if we look at the comparative fit index (CFI) or Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI), we can see the values are well below the recommended .90 cutoff, and if we scroll down, we can see the RMSEA output with the estimated root mean square error of approximation and 90% CI, as well as a hypothesis test that the RMSEA is equal to or greater than .05. A significant value would be ideal, but this may be affected by sample size. Based on the RMSEA estimate and width of the CI, we would want to see values below .10 to indicate better fit. The SRMR does seem to be acceptable, but by other methods, it appears that this model fit is not good.

    If we scroll down, we can look at the estimates for factor loadings and their statistical significance. Note that to set the scale for loadings, the first unstandardized loading of each factor - seen here on the left - is set to 1.00. The standardized estimates we asked for are on the far-right column. Significance testing is in the p-value column, which will tell you whether the item is significantly predicted by its specified latent variable. You can interpret these standardized and unstandardized estimates the same way you would interpret a regression coefficient, where the item is the dependent variable, Y, and the latent variable factor score is X.

    # Specify a model with correlated errors (I have chosen errors at random just for an example)
correlatederrormod <- 'factor =~ GS2 + GS4 + GS5 + GS6 + GS7 + GS8 + GS9 + GS12
                GS2 ~~ GS4
                GS5 ~~ GS9'
correlatederror <- cfa(correlatederrormod, data = grit)
summary(correlatederror, fit.measures = T, standardized = T)
# Now you'll see the item covariances as part of the output as well

    Categorical Items

    It should also be noted that categorical items cannot be linearly associated, so categorical items should be fit to a CFA using polychoric correlations rather than traditional methods. Different simulations have postulated different numbers of response options to be acceptably treated as continuous. While some simulations have produced mixed results about the number of response options that can reasonably be treated as continuous, typically 4 options or fewer are more likely to produce higher bias. Simulations have produced mixed results for 5 items, but 6 or more items can usually be considered continuous without producing bias (Rhemtulla et al, 2012).

    “Specifically, because product-moment covariances or correlations measure linear associations, they often provide very inaccurate estimates of the bivariate associations among binary or ordinal variables, which then leads to inaccurate CFA results (see Flora, LaBrish, & Chalmers, 2012, for a demonstration); just as binary or ordinal logistic regression is recommended over linear multiple regression for a categorical outcome, a categorical-variable method is recommended for factor analysis when the observed item scores are categorical. Therefore, it is important to account for the categorical nature of the item scores, which is commonly done by fitting the factor model to polychoric correlations (see Finney & DiStefano, 2013).” - Flora (2020 - https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/2515245920951747)

    To fit a model using polychoric correlations, you can specify items as ordered using “ordered = T”, and lavaan will automatically recognize that it should use polychoric correlations. By recommendations by Rhemtulla and colleagues (2012), given a high sample size and 5 response options, I will be fitting these data using polychoric correlations for remaining models.

    Two-Factor Model

    The one-factor model produced a poor fit, indicating that a single factor does not well explain the GRIT. Instead, we can test a two-factor model that represents constructs of Consistency of Interest and Perseverance of Effort. To specify a two-factor model, we can write the code the same way we did with the one-factor model, but with one line specifying each factor. The factors will automatically be allowed to correlate.

    # Specify two-factor model
twofactormod <- 'COI =~ GS2 + GS5 + GS7 + GS8
                POE =~ GS4 + GS6 + GS9 + GS12'
twofactor <- cfa(twofactormod, data = grit, ordered = T)
summary(twofactor, fit.measures = T, standardized = T)

    While the chi-square test is still significant, we can see that our fit indices that are less sensitive to sample size have shown a lot of improvement. CFI and TLI have moved into a more acceptable range, though RMSEA is still higher than we would like to see.

    Once again, you can scroll down to look at the estimates, so you can see that the estimates for each of the items under their respective factor. Below, there's also a covariances section, which shows the covariance between the two factors. In this case, they are negatively covaried and the p-value is significant, suggesting as one increases, the other decreases.

    Bifactor Model and Model Comparison

    We can also test bifactor models, which are increasingly prevalent in recent years. A bifactor model includes one general factor to capture shared variance among all the items and one or more specific factors capturing residual variance among subsets of items that remains over and above the general factor. When specifying the model, we will have a line for the general factor and one for each of the specific factors. We must also specify that the factors are orthogonal by stating that their covariances are constrained to 0.

    # Specify a bifactor model
bifactormod <- 'GRIT =~ GS2 + GS4 + GS5 + GS6 + GS7 + GS8 + GS9 + GS12
                GS2 ~~ GS4
                COI =~ GS2 + GS5 + GS7 + GS8
                POE =~ GS4 + GS6 + GS9 + GS12
                GRIT ~~ 0*COI + 0*POE
                COI ~~ 0*POE'
bifactor <- cfa(bifactormod, data = grit, ordered = T)
summary(bifactor, fit.measures = T, standardized = T)

    So far, this seems to be the best fitting model, based on fit indices. However, if we wanted to test whether it is significantly better of a fit than a simpler model like the two-factor, we could use the same anova() function we used last week to run a chi-square difference test.

    # Test which model is better
anova(twofactor, bifactor)

    Higher-Order Model

    Finally, another common model is the higher-order model. In the case of the GRIT, the higher-order model is not identified. However, if it was identified, you could specify the model as the following:

    higherordermod <- 'COI =~ GS2 + GS5 + GS7 + GS8
                  POE =~ GS4 + GS6 + GS9 + GS12
                  GRIT =~ COI + POE'
higherorder <- cfa(higherordermod, data = grit, ordered = T)
summary(higherorder, fit.measures = T, standardized = T)

    Path Diagrams

    You can also easily make the path diagrams for your using lavaanPlot or semPaths. As usual, these plots can be further customized for font size, colour, shape, etc. with options further explored in package outlines: lavaanPlot: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/lavaanPlot/lavaanPlot.pdf semPaths: http://sachaepskamp.com/documentation/semPlot/semPaths.html or https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/semPlot/semPlot.pdf

    # Plot our path diagram for the two-factor model
# "coefs = T" will give the path coefficients
# "stand = T" will standardize path coefficients
lavaanPlot(model = twofactor, coefs = T, stand = T)

# Plot the bifactor model
# I find it easier to use semPaths when plotting a bifactor model, as it produces nicer diagrams for the bifactor setup but this is personal preference
# To do this, you have to specify layout as "tree2" or "tree3"
# You'll also need to use bifactor = "x" (where "x" is the name of your general factor) to specify which factor to treat as the general factor
semPaths(bifactor, what = "paths", layout = "tree3", bifactor = "GRIT")
